screens.title: Building and Programming a Physical Rover
screens.narratorSegment: In this unit you will bring simulation skills into the real world by building a small autonomous rover with a Raspberry Pi, motor driver, motors, and sensors. You'll learn how the Pi acts as the robot's brain, why a separate motor driver is required to safely power DC motors, and how sensors like an ultrasonic rangefinder and IMU let the rover detect and respond to its surroundings. We'll also cover practical topics: powering the Pi and motors separately, wiring common GPIO mappings, and logging sensor and motor data for debugging after a run. A concrete early milestone will be a simple script that makes the rover drive forward and turn when an obstacle is detected. Along the way you will practice safety checks for batteries and motor wiring, and learn a standard test sequence to validate each subsystem before integrated runs. By the end you will understand both the hardware layout and the software loop that makes a rover behave autonomously, and you’ll be ready to iterate on sensing and behaviors with data-driven tweaks. What sensor might you add next to improve navigation?

Practical Skills & Safety

Step 1

screens.title: Raspberry Pi and Motor Driver Roles
screens.narratorSegment: A critical design principle is separating logic-level control from high-current motor power. The Raspberry Pi runs Linux and executes your Python control loop; it provides GPIO signals that indicate motor direction and request speed via PWM. However, a Pi's GPIO pins can only supply a few milliamps and cannot safely power DC motors, which draw hundreds of milliamps or even amps at startup. The motor driver — such as the L298N or TB6612FNG — acts as an intermediary with transistors or H-bridges that switch the higher currents the motors require while accepting low-current logic inputs from the Pi. A concrete example: the Pi asserts a forward signal on a GPIO pin. The driver reads that logic level and supplies current from the motor battery to the motor terminals. A common misconception is to think that PWM from the Pi powers the motor directly; in reality PWM is a control signal that the driver converts to actual motor voltage and current. Key practical consequences: keep the Pi on a stable USB power bank, give motors a separate battery pack, and test driver inputs with LEDs or small loads before connecting motors. How does isolating power reduce the chance of resets and hardware damage?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Pi & Motor Driver
Definition

Logic vs Power

The Pi provides logic-level signals. The motor driver provides switched power and direction control to the motors.

Raspberry Pi
Runs Python, reads sensors, toggles GPIO and PWM outputs.
Motor Driver
Handles higher voltages/currents, protects the Pi, and supplies motor power.
Analogy

Think of the Pi as the driver giving steering signals and the motor driver as the engine delivering force to the wheels.

Wiring Snapshot
Control Signals
  • GPIO pins for direction and enable
  • PWM input for speed control
  • Ground shared between Pi and driver
Power Connections
  • Motor battery to driver Vmotor
  • Pi powered by USB bank
  • Separate supplies prevent voltage drop on Pi
Check Your Understanding
Why must the Pi and motor battery share ground even though their supplies are separate?

screens.title: Wiring the Rover Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Wiring a rover is best done in small, verifiable steps. Start by mounting the components to the chassis and laying out wiring so power and signal cables are tidy. First, connect grounds: the Pi ground and the motor driver ground must be common so logic references line up. Second, wire the motor driver's control inputs to chosen GPIO pins. In the chapter example, direction pins might map to GPIO 17, 18, 22, and 23, and ultrasonic trigger and echo to 24 and 25. Third, attach the motor power supply to the driver, keeping Pi power separate. Before attaching motors, run a low-voltage LED or small tester on driver outputs to confirm responses to control signals. Fourth, connect sensors: ultrasonic trigger and echo require one output and one input; the IMU connects via I2C to SDA and SCL pins. As a final verification, use a simple script to toggle each GPIO and read each sensor in isolation. A common misconception is to skip the ground step; without a common reference the driver and Pi will not agree on high and low signals, leading to unpredictable behavior. After wiring, label wires and preserve a short, repeatable test checklist to reduce later debugging time.

Process Flow

Staged wiring and verification

Step 1
Mount parts, run grounds common to Pi and driver.
Step 2
Wire driver inputs to GPIO (example pins: 17,18,22,23).
Step 3
Attach motor power to driver; keep Pi on separate USB bank.

screens.title: Sensors: Ultrasonic, IR, IMU, Camera
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing what your sensors actually measure and their limitations helps you design reliable behaviors. The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance by sending a sound pulse and timing the echo. It is inexpensive and easy to use but struggles with soft or angled surfaces that absorb or deflect sound. Infrared proximity sensors are better for short-range detection and edge sensing, such as spotting table edges, but they typically have shorter range and are more affected by surface reflectivity. An IMU like the MPU6050 gives acceleration and angular velocity, useful for detecting collisions, sudden acceleration events, or estimate orientation when fused over time. The Pi Camera module provides visual feedback for line following or object detection but is optional and adds complexity. A common misconception is assuming a single sensor gives a complete picture; instead, combine sensors for robustness. For example, use ultrasonic for mid-range obstacles and IR for cliff detection. When testing, measure ultrasonic readings against a ruler and note how soft materials return smaller or inconsistent distances. Thinking about where sensors fail guides where to add redundancy or adjust the behavior thresholds.

Definition

Sensor roles and limits

HC-SR04 Ultrasonic

screens.title: Ultrasonic Range Measurement and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor estimates distance by sending a short pulse of sound and measuring the time until an echo returns. The sensor triggers a pulse, then the echo pin flips when the echo is received; time difference converts to distance using the speed of sound. This method is straightforward in controlled settings but can produce incorrect readings for multiple reasons. Soft materials can absorb the sound, producing little or no echo. Angled surfaces deflect the pulse away from the sensor. Multiple nearby surfaces can cause confusing echoes and false short readings. Temperature also affects the speed of sound; the simple calculation assumes a fixed speed, so extreme conditions introduce small errors. A practical test is to compare the sensor's readout to a ruler at multiple distances and materials. A common misconception is that a single anomalous reading means the sensor is broken; often the environment caused the echo to be missed or misinterpreted. To mitigate these issues, filter readings over several measurements, ignore spikes, and combine ultrasonic data with an IR sensor or IMU event to confirm obstacle presence. How might you smooth occasional false readings in a control loop?

Definition

How ultrasonic distance sensing works

Measurement
Send a pulse, time the echo, convert time to distance using sound speed.
Common Pitfalls
Soft/angled surfaces, multiple reflections, and temperature variations can cause wrong distances.
Test
Compare sensor readings with a ruler at several distances and materials.
Filter
Apply a moving average or median filter to ignore spikes before deciding on actions.
Combine
Use IR or IMU events to corroborate ultrasonic readings for robust detection.
Key Takeaway

Treat ultrasonic data as one input among several and validate with tests and filters before making motor decisions.

screens.title: PWM and Motor Speed Control
screens.narratorSegment: Pulse-width modulation, or PWM, is the standard method to control motor speed in microcomputer-driven robots. The Pi generates a square wave on a GPIO pin where the duty cycle determines the average voltage seen by the motor through the driver; for example, a 60 percent duty cycle delivers more effective power and a faster wheel speed than a 30 percent duty cycle. Because the Pi's GPIO cannot source motor current, the PWM is interpreted by the motor driver which switches the higher motor voltage accordingly. Two practical notes: first, PWM frequency and the driver's capabilities affect torque smoothness; second, abrupt changes in duty cycle can cause large current spikes at motor startup. A common contrast is PWM control vs fixed-voltage control: PWM allows fine-grained speed control without requiring variable supply voltages. A typical error is commanding full duty cycle immediately; instead ramp speed gently during tests. For precise odometry, combine motor encoders with PWM commands; PWM alone does not guarantee a specific wheel rotation when load and battery voltage vary. PWM and Motor Speed Control means pwm sets motor effective power through the driver; combine it with encoders for precise motion under varying loads.. In practical terms, how pwm from the pi translates to motor speed via the driver. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › PWM Control
Comparison

PWM vs Fixed Voltage

PWM (with driver)
  • Duty cycle controls average motor power.
  • Driver translates low-current PWM into high-current switching.
  • Suitable for fine speed control without changing supply.
Fixed voltage
  • Speed varies with load and battery voltage.
  • Less flexible without additional electronics.
  • Often used only for simple on/off movements.
Test Tip
Ramp PWM gradually to avoid high inrush currents and resets.
Encoder Note
Combine encoders with PWM for closed-loop speed or distance control.
Common Mistake
Assuming duty cycle equals wheel RPM; load and battery state change actual speed.
Key Takeaway

Use PWM as a command to the driver and pair it with sensors or encoders when you need predictable motion under load.

screens.title: Python Control Loop Example
screens.narratorSegment: We now look at a concise Python control loop that ties the hardware together. The script configures GPIO pins for motor direction and for the ultrasonic trigger and echo, defines a function to set motor speed using simple direction outputs, and measures distance by sending a short trigger pulse and timing the echo. In the main loop it repeatedly reads distance, prints the value for logging, and chooses an action: if an obstacle is closer than a threshold it commands a turning motion for a short period, otherwise it drives forward. The concrete example demonstrates reactive control: sensor input immediately affects motor commands without building a map. One misconception to avoid is treating print statements as a substitute for formal logging; for later analysis you should write structured CSV or logging output. Also do not forget to call the GPIO cleanup routine to restore pin states when exiting. This script is purposely simple to show the core loop; you can later enhance it with PWM speed control, smoothing filters on sensor readings, and data logging to CSV for post-run analysis. What would you log every loop iteration to help diagnose misbehavior?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Python Example
Code Walkthrough

Simple obstacle-avoidance script

import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
import time

# Motor pins
MOTOR_A_FWD = 17
MOTOR_A_BWD = 18
MOTOR_B_FWD = 22
MOTOR_B_BWD = 23

# Ultrasonic sensor pins
TRIG = 24
ECHO = 25

GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
for pin in [MOTOR_A_FWD, MOTOR_A_BWD, MOTOR_B_FWD, MOTOR_B_BWD]:
    GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.OUT)
GPIO.setup(TRIG, GPIO.OUT)
GPIO.setup(ECHO, GPIO.IN)

def set_motor_speed(left_speed, right_speed):
    # left_speed and right_speed: -1 to 1
    GPIO.output(MOTOR_A_FWD, left_speed > 0)
    GPIO.output(MOTOR_A_BWD, left_speed < 0)
    GPIO.output(MOTOR_B_FWD, right_speed > 0)
    GPIO.output(MOTOR_B_BWD, right_speed < 0)

def read_distance():
    GPIO.output(TRIG, True)
    time.sleep(0.00001)
    GPIO.output(TRIG, False)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    while GPIO.input(ECHO) == 0:
        start_time = time.time()
    
    end_time = time.time()
    while GPIO.input(ECHO) == 1:
        end_time = time.time()
    
    distance = (end_time - start_time) * 34300 / 2
    return distance

# Simple obstacle avoidance
if __name__ == '__main__':
    try:
        while True:
            dist = read_distance()
            print(f"Distance: {dist:.1f} cm")
            
            if dist < 20:  # Obstacle detected within 20 cm
                set_motor_speed(-0.5, 0.5)  # Turn left
                time.sleep(0.5)
            else:
                set_motor_speed(0.6, 0.6)  # Move forward
            
            time.sleep(0.1)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        GPIO.cleanup()
Explanation
  • Setup pins for motors and ultrasonic, set BCM numbering.
  • set_motor_speed sets direction bits; PWM can replace boolean outputs for speed.
  • read_distance sends a trigger, times echo, and computes distance using sound speed.
  • Main loop prints distance and chooses between forward or turn behavior.
Example Extension
Replace print statements with CSV logging: timestamp, distance, left_speed, right_speed. This helps plot and analyze runs afterwards.
Key Takeaway

Start with a simple reactive loop, then add smoothing, PWM speed control, and structured logging for iteration.

screens.title: Implementing Obstacle Avoidance Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Obstacle avoidance is the foundational autonomous behavior for a basic rover. The simplest reactive approach is a bug algorithm: drive forward until a sensor detects an obstacle within a threshold, then perform an avoidance maneuver such as rotating for a short period before resuming forward motion. Another pattern is wall following, where the rover maintains a roughly constant distance to a wall using side sensors. Random walk with obstacle avoidance uses random headings and avoids collisions, useful for exploration without mapping. Light following and line following are other behaviors that require specialized sensors. A concrete implementation detail from the chapter: use an ultrasonic threshold of about 20 centimeters to trigger a turn, then command differential wheel speeds to rotate. A common misconception is to expect these reactive strategies to navigate complex environments; they work in constrained spaces but do not build maps or keep global position. The practical next steps are to log each sensor reading and motor command so you can plot how often avoidance triggers and tune thresholds. Consider adding a short state machine in code to prevent oscillation, for example a brief pause after a turn to allow sensor readings to stabilize.

screens.title: Data Logging for Debugging and Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Logging is essential when behavior in the real world diverges from expectation. A minimal log entry includes a timestamp, the distance reading from the ultrasonic sensor, the commanded left and right motor speeds, and any state flags such as 'turning' or 'cooldown'. Save entries to a CSV file or use Python's logging module with structured messages; CSV is simple and easy to plot later. Having a time-aligned record lets you correlate sensor spikes with motor commands and observe how often avoidance events occur. For example, if the rover frequently triggers avoidance at the same distance but then fails to clear the obstacle, the log will show repeated short rotations and immediate retriggers, indicating the need for a longer turn or cooldown. Another benefit is reproducibility: you can replay the log to simulate the robot's inputs in software or when plotting in Python or MATLAB. A common misconception is that console prints are sufficient; prints lack consistent formatting and timestamps unless you add them intentionally. Structured logging makes post-run analysis, parameter tuning, and regression checks far easier. screens.title: Testing Checklist and Safety Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Before you run the rover for the first time, follow a short checklist to reduce the chance of damage or unstable operation. Verify that all wires are secure and insulated, the motor battery is appropriate for the driver and motors, and the Pi's USB bank is charged. Confirm that grounds are common and that no pins are shorted. Run a brief motor driver test at low duty cycle to ensure correct spin directions, and verify that wheels are free of obstructions. For battery safety, ensure LiPo batteries — if used — have protection circuits and are never shorted; prefer AA packs for early testing when possible. Add a power switch or an accessible emergency stop to cut power quickly. Test sensors separately: check that ultrasonic returns correlate with a ruler and check IMU responses when gently moving the chassis. A common misconception is rushing to integrated tests; staged verification saves time by isolating faults quickly. Keep a clear testing area to avoid damage, and start on a flat surface to prevent accidental falls. These simple habits protect your hardware and let you focus on algorithm development.

fullNarratorScript:
In this unit you will bring simulation skills into the real world by building a small autonomous rover with a Raspberry Pi, motor driver, motors, and sensors. You'll learn how the Pi acts as the robot's brain, why a separate motor driver is required to safely power DC motors, and how sensors like an ultrasonic rangefinder and IMU let the rover detect and respond to its surroundings. We'll also cover practical topics: powering the Pi and motors separately, wiring common GPIO mappings, and logging sensor and motor data for debugging after a run. A concrete early milestone will be a simple script that makes the rover drive forward and turn when an obstacle is detected. Along the way you will practice safety checks for batteries and motor wiring, and learn a standard test sequence to validate each subsystem before integrated runs. By the end you will understand both the hardware layout and the software loop that makes a rover behave autonomously, and you’ll be ready to iterate on sensing and behaviors with data-driven tweaks. What sensor might you add next to improve navigation?

These objectives outline the practical skills and reasoning you will practice while building the rover. First, you will assemble the physical system from a Raspberry Pi, motor driver, DC motors, wheels, and sensors so you understand how each component contributes. Hands-on assembly builds intuition about mechanical constraints and wiring safety. Second, you will program the Raspberry Pi in Python to read sensors and command motors using GPIO and PWM. Writing that control loop shows how sensor readings translate to real-world motion. Third, you will implement a simple autonomous behavior: obstacle avoidance driven by an ultrasonic or IR sensor. This introduces reactive algorithms that work without a map. Fourth, you will log sensor data and motor commands so you can debug and analyze behavior after a run. Logging converts noisy, transient events into data you can inspect and improve. Each objective includes a milestone that verifies competency and helps you incrementally integrate hardware and software in a reproducible way.

This second objectives slide focuses on testing, safety, and integration practices you will adopt. You will learn correct wiring and the reason for separating motor power from the Raspberry Pi's supply, which prevents voltage drops and resets. You will verify GPIO mappings by running small scripts that toggle outputs before connecting motors. You will test each sensor — measure ultrasonic distance against a ruler and check IMU values when you tap the robot — to confirm expected responses. You will adopt a staged test plan: power checks, motor driver test at low duty cycle, sensor sanity checks, then integrated behavior testing on a flat surface. The safety objective includes battery handling: use a power switch, avoid short circuits, and apply LiPo protection circuits when applicable. Each of these steps is a small verification milestone that reduces risk and makes debugging faster when behaviors don't match expectations.

A critical design principle is separating logic-level control from high-current motor power. The Raspberry Pi runs Linux and executes your Python control loop; it provides GPIO signals that indicate motor direction and request speed via PWM. However, a Pi's GPIO pins can only supply a few milliamps and cannot safely power DC motors, which draw hundreds of milliamps or even amps at startup. The motor driver — such as the L298N or TB6612FNG — acts as an intermediary with transistors or H-bridges that switch the higher currents the motors require while accepting low-current logic inputs from the Pi. A concrete example: the Pi asserts a forward signal on a GPIO pin. The driver reads that logic level and supplies current from the motor battery to the motor terminals. A common misconception is to think that PWM from the Pi powers the motor directly; in reality PWM is a control signal that the driver converts to actual motor voltage and current. Key practical consequences: keep the Pi on a stable USB power bank, give motors a separate battery pack, and test driver inputs with LEDs or small loads before connecting motors. How does isolating power reduce the chance of resets and hardware damage?

Wiring a rover is best done in small, verifiable steps. Start by mounting the components to the chassis and laying out wiring so power and signal cables are tidy. First, connect grounds: the Pi ground and the motor driver ground must be common so logic references line up. Second, wire the motor driver's control inputs to chosen GPIO pins. In the chapter example, direction pins might map to GPIO 17, 18, 22, and 23, and ultrasonic trigger and echo to 24 and 25. Third, attach the motor power supply to the driver, keeping Pi power separate. Before attaching motors, run a low-voltage LED or small tester on driver outputs to confirm responses to control signals. Fourth, connect sensors: ultrasonic trigger and echo require one output and one input; the IMU connects via I2C to SDA and SCL pins. As a final verification, use a simple script to toggle each GPIO and read each sensor in isolation. A common misconception is to skip the ground step; without a common reference the driver and Pi will not agree on high and low signals, leading to unpredictable behavior. After wiring, label wires and preserve a short, repeatable test checklist to reduce later debugging time.

Knowing what your sensors actually measure and their limitations helps you design reliable behaviors. The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance by sending a sound pulse and timing the echo. It is inexpensive and easy to use but struggles with soft or angled surfaces that absorb or deflect sound. Infrared proximity sensors are better for short-range detection and edge sensing, such as spotting table edges, but they typically have shorter range and are more affected by surface reflectivity. An IMU like the MPU6050 gives acceleration and angular velocity, useful for detecting collisions, sudden acceleration events, or estimate orientation when fused over time. The Pi Camera module provides visual feedback for line following or object detection but is optional and adds complexity. A common misconception is assuming a single sensor gives a complete picture; instead, combine sensors for robustness. For example, use ultrasonic for mid-range obstacles and IR for cliff detection. When testing, measure ultrasonic readings against a ruler and note how soft materials return smaller or inconsistent distances. Thinking about where sensors fail guides where to add redundancy or adjust the behavior thresholds.

The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor estimates distance by sending a short pulse of sound and measuring the time until an echo returns. The sensor triggers a pulse, then the echo pin flips when the echo is received; time difference converts to distance using the speed of sound. This method is straightforward in controlled settings but can produce incorrect readings for multiple reasons. Soft materials can absorb the sound, producing little or no echo. Angled surfaces deflect the pulse away from the sensor. Multiple nearby surfaces can cause confusing echoes and false short readings. Temperature also affects the speed of sound; the simple calculation assumes a fixed speed, so extreme conditions introduce small errors. A practical test is to compare the sensor's readout to a ruler at multiple distances and materials. A common misconception is that a single anomalous reading means the sensor is broken; often the environment caused the echo to be missed or misinterpreted. To mitigate these issues, filter readings over several measurements, ignore spikes, and combine ultrasonic data with an IR sensor or IMU event to confirm obstacle presence. How might you smooth occasional false readings in a control loop?

Pulse-width modulation, or PWM, is the standard method to control motor speed in microcomputer-driven robots. The Pi generates a square wave on a GPIO pin where the duty cycle determines the average voltage seen by the motor through the driver; for example, a 60 percent duty cycle delivers more effective power and a faster wheel speed than a 30 percent duty cycle. Because the Pi's GPIO cannot source motor current, the PWM is interpreted by the motor driver which switches the higher motor voltage accordingly. Two practical notes: first, PWM frequency and the driver's capabilities affect torque smoothness; second, abrupt changes in duty cycle can cause large current spikes at motor startup. A common contrast is PWM control vs fixed-voltage control: PWM allows fine-grained speed control without requiring variable supply voltages. A typical error is commanding full duty cycle immediately; instead ramp speed gently during tests. For precise odometry, combine motor encoders with PWM commands; PWM alone does not guarantee a specific wheel rotation when load and battery voltage vary. PWM and Motor Speed Control means pwm sets motor effective power through the driver; combine it with encoders for precise motion under varying loads.. In practical terms, how pwm from the pi translates to motor speed via the driver. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We now look at a concise Python control loop that ties the hardware together. The script configures GPIO pins for motor direction and for the ultrasonic trigger and echo, defines a function to set motor speed using simple direction outputs, and measures distance by sending a short trigger pulse and timing the echo. In the main loop it repeatedly reads distance, prints the value for logging, and chooses an action: if an obstacle is closer than a threshold it commands a turning motion for a short period, otherwise it drives forward. The concrete example demonstrates reactive control: sensor input immediately affects motor commands without building a map. One misconception to avoid is treating print statements as a substitute for formal logging; for later analysis you should write structured CSV or logging output. Also do not forget to call the GPIO cleanup routine to restore pin states when exiting. This script is purposely simple to show the core loop; you can later enhance it with PWM speed control, smoothing filters on sensor readings, and data logging to CSV for post-run analysis. What would you log every loop iteration to help diagnose misbehavior?

Obstacle avoidance is the foundational autonomous behavior for a basic rover. The simplest reactive approach is a bug algorithm: drive forward until a sensor detects an obstacle within a threshold, then perform an avoidance maneuver such as rotating for a short period before resuming forward motion. Another pattern is wall following, where the rover maintains a roughly constant distance to a wall using side sensors. Random walk with obstacle avoidance uses random headings and avoids collisions, useful for exploration without mapping. Light following and line following are other behaviors that require specialized sensors.
